signals.headline: £91.6m EFS balance utilised at end 25/26 + further £65.3m Capitalisation Direction requested for 26/27 and 27/28; target of balancing without EFS from 2028/29
signals.why_it_matters: Slough is one of the small group of authorities still actively drawing under EFS following its 2021 S114. The paper is unusually specific about the borrowing consequences of this — quantifying assumed DSG-driven borrowing (£5m in 26/27, £20m in 27/28) inside the debt-repayment model.

signals.headline: £55.6m new borrowing in 26/27 rising to £189.0m in 28/29 assumed at 5% PWLB EIP
signals.why_it_matters: Table 3 forecasts a very substantial drawdown programme across 26/27-30/31, bridged by the two-pool liability benchmark. New-borrowing rate assumption (5%) sits below the current Arlingclose PWLB certainty implied rate for 10y (~5.32%) but above HRA (~4.92%).

Whether the FMS call at Slough held or was called cannot be determined from this paper — recorded as a fact worth watching in future outturn.

signals.why_it_matters: Explicit quantification of expected borrowing to service the DSG deficit is unusually specific disclosure — most papers give the DSG risk qualitatively. The paper does not name a statutory override end date.

summary.text:
A distressed-authority strategy handled more transparently than many. Slough is five years on from its July 2021 S114 and still inside its Exceptional Financial Support agreement: £91.6m of Capitalisation Direction borrowing utilised by the end of 25/26, out of an original £352.2m envelope reduced by £227.8m of disposal receipts and £32.8m of MRP. The paper flags a further £65.3m of EFS in-principle for 26/27 and 27/28, targeting a balanced budget without EFS from 2028/29. Capital receipts of £79.4m over the next three years are the plan for keeping that trajectory on track.

What stands out among the papers we're reading this strategy season is the explicit £5m (26/27) and £20m (27/28) borrowing assumption to fund the DSG overspend, named in the Debt Repayment Strategy appendix at 87146 p.4. Most councils treat DSG as a qualitative risk with no borrowing figure attached; Slough puts it in the model. The strategy also prints an unusually candid per-capita comparator — £2,914.40 for Slough against a 15-council sample average of £1,924.21 — and sets its own target of GF debt below £300m within ten years. The 10-year model (87146 p.6) reaches that target only in year 9 (34/35), and never brings the financing-cost ratio below the 10% target.

Loan book at 31.12.25 is £443.7m at weighted 3.5691% (Appendix D), split £321.24m GF at 3.6240% and £122.41m HRA at 3.4251%. Composition: PWLB £416.8m + LOBOs £9m + Bank £4m at the start of 26/27, with £55.6m of new borrowing forecast in 26/27 rising to £189m in 28/29. LOBO position: three instruments — FMS Wertmanagement £5m at 3.99%, Dexia £4m at 3.75%, Barclays £4m at 4.76% (App D labels Barclays 'Fixed'; may be historic LOBO now fixed). The paper's own note at §15.2 flags the 07 April 2026 call opportunity on the FMS £5m — that date is now past, and whether it was called or held is not testable from the paper.

Balance-sheet identity checks. CFR £686.0m less external borrowing £485.4m less PFI/leases £30.9m (from Table 8/9) = £169.7m internal borrowing on the strict CIPFA formula. The paper prints £200.6m, using a narrower definition of external borrowing that excludes PFI/leases. Both self-consistent; £30.9m of definitional gap is exactly the PFI/leases figure. Two-pool liability benchmark: GF £383.5m at 31.3.26 (opening 26/27 £384.13m in the debt-repayment model), HRA £101.9m. Both benchmarks decline steeply to c.2075 as the existing book runs off.

Financing-cost ratios sit high (GF 14.5% at 31.3.26; HRA 8.0%) and stay above the paper's own 10% target in every year the model runs. The MRP policy on post-2008 capex uses the annuity method with the interest rate set to the average PWLB long-term rate in the year the asset becomes operational (§42.1) — a series we publish daily. Company-lending exposure is £57.8m, dominated by James Elliman Homes at £51.7m; investment income is expressly earmarked against a loss provision (§48.1).

Reconciliation with our PWLB file FAILS. Our price_book at 31.12.25 returns 13 loans totalling £153.94m; paper Appendix D carries ~£430.65m of PWLB across 42 rows. Gap ~£276.7m — over 60% of the book. Our live maturity snapshot at 2026-08-16 shows 39 loans of £456.5m, larger than the historical 'as-at' figure, so the as-at logic is filtering by drawdown-date metadata our file does not hold for the pre-existing long-dated tail. Same shape as the Leicester and Redcar reconciliation failures. Recorded in the note per PIPELINE.md; kept out of the email; coverage gap disclosed once without inviting correction; break-cost figures held for the same reason. The email leans on qualitative content — the DSG disclosure, the LOBO cross-council pattern, the moved Arlingclose forecast, and the MRP-rate-series connection.

officer.subject: The £5m and £20m DSG borrowing you've quantified — and a note on the April LOBO call
officer.body:
Dear Executive Director of Resources,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 and the Debt Repayment Strategy that went to Full Council on 26 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and given the position Slough is working through, this is offered in the spirit of what may be useful rather than as a critique. The strategy and the debt-repayment appendix are among the more candid pieces of work we've read this season.

What drew our attention first is that the Debt Repayment Strategy puts a number on the DSG borrowing — £5m in 26/27 and £20m in 27/28 (87146 p.4). Most treasury papers we read leave the DSG deficit as a qualitative risk without an amount attached; putting the assumed borrowing into the model, and being explicit that the borrowing is a GF cost, is unusual disclosure. So is the per-capita comparator on p.1 — £2,914.40 for Slough against a 15-council sample average of £1,924.21 — which very few authorities put on the face of their own paper. Members draw their conclusions from your numbers rather than someone else's.

Second, and only because §15.2 names the date: the £5m FMS Wertmanagement LOBO had a call opportunity on 7 April 2026, four months back. We can't see from the paper whether it was called or held. What we can see across the councils we've read this year is a pattern — twelve LOBO calls have landed in the same window and every one has been declined by the lender. Dexia's calls at Kent and Tameside, three refused at Wolverhampton, one at Staffordshire, KBC's two loans at Bath & NE Somerset going floating with six-monthly resets rather than a rate rise, among others. Twelve for twelve. Context for what your paper flags, and something no single council can see on its own.

Appendix C leans on the Arlingclose central case from 22 December 2025 — Bank Rate cut to 3.25% by the middle of 2026, held at 3.25% for three years. Six months on, Bank Rate is still 3.75%: no cut since December, and June came and went without one. Arlingclose's note flagged that near-term upside risks had increased, so this isn't a surprise, but it does mean the 5% new-borrowing assumption at §4.2 sits against a 10-year PWLB certainty rate around 5.8% today. Your own advisor has it easing back to about 5.1% by September, so the 5% reads as consistent with the forecast you printed rather than the curve as it stands. On HRA the 40bp discount gets you to about 5.4% today against 4.7% on that forecast path. The full curve is at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard.

One closer connection. Your MRP policy at §42.1 uses the annuity method for post-2008 capex 'with the interest rate set to the average PWLB long-term rate in the year the asset becomes operational' — that is a series we publish daily, and holding the annuity-rate history for every asset year in one place is a piece of housekeeping the platform can carry.

Where you might find us most useful day-to-day is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, which prices every published council's PWLB book against the DMO's premature-repayment curve. One caveat before you look: our file for Slough is missing the historic long-dated tail behind the £443.7m in your Appendix D — the same gap we've seen at Leicester and Redcar, where the file anchors to newer drawdown metadata. Anything drawn during this strategy period, and the monthly sector totals at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity, we can benchmark with confidence.

Standing point, because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151: the liability benchmark pathway is becoming central to how the whole strategy is framed. Your two-pool set-up in Tables 6 and 7 (GF £383.5m, HRA £101.9m at 31.3.26) is one of the cleaner treatments we've read. An interactive version tied to our live rate feeds sits at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — for a GF pool Table 6 shows £55.6m under its benchmark at 31.3.26 and £189.0m under it by 31.3.30, being able to move the reserves and cost-of-carry paths and see the crossover shift is the useful thing.

On training, four look most relevant to Slough. After the S114: capitalisation & EFS is written directly for the position you're managing through. LOBO loans (legacy) covers the mechanics of what happens when a call date lands. HRA Liability Benchmark: two-pool sits on Tables 6 and 7. MRP — policy options and revenue impact ties to the annuity approach at §42.1. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts are available for the whole team.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
